title: Lesson 5 (Part 1): Speaking – Introductions
concepts:
• Useful Language: Reasons: because, as, one reason is (that) … / Examples: for example, such as.
• Speaking Skill: A good answer is full, descriptive and gives a reason or an example – not just one word.
pre_learning:
• Actions: Write your answers to three interview questions on the board (e.g. By car. / Football. / Twice a week.). Students guess the questions (How do you get to school? …). Explain that today’s lesson is about answering such questions well.
• Assessment: Check students can form correct present simple questions.
outcomes:
• Ask and answer questions to give personal information (name, address, free time).
• Evaluate two candidates’ answers and explain why one is better.
• Extend answers by giving reasons and examples (because, as, one reason is that, for example).
• Take part in a short interview (B1 Preliminary Speaking Part 1 style).
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book p. 19 (Ex 1–9); Audio 1.05, 1.06; Practice Guide p. 83; board
Step 1: Personal information 8 min
   - Ex 1: Students answer the questions for themselves; clarify full name / surname / middle name.
   - Ex 2: Pairs ask each other questions and complete the table about their partner, then check spelling together.
Step 2: Listening & evaluating answers 14 min
   - Ex 3: Play Audio 1.05. Who gives the better answer? → Chen (fuller, more descriptive).
   - Ex 4: Using the useful language box, pairs improve Huda’s answer (where exactly she lives, why she likes it).
   - Ex 5–6: Play Audio 1.06. → Huda gives the better answer this time. Pairs plan how Chen could extend his answer with reasons and examples.
Step 3: Practice task 15 min
   - Ex 7: Students think about how to extend their answers, then interview each other.
   - Ex 8: Fact file – the teacher answers as a famous Omani person; students then do the same in pairs (they may invent details).
   - Ex 9 (Speaking extra): New pairs, new questions; monitor and note good language and common errors.
formative: Peer feedback: while one student answers, the partner ticks a simple checklist on paper – full answer ✓, reason ✓, example ✓. Partners share one strength and one suggestion.
closing: Reasons chain in groups of six: Statement on the board (e.g. Learning English is useful.). Each student adds a different reason (One reason is … / Another reason is … / Also …); a student who can’t think of one is out.
homework: Write answers to three interview questions about yourself, giving a reason or an example in each answer.

• Actions: Write: I really enjoy watching … because … / Something I hate watching is … because … . Students complete both sentences and compare in pairs. Find out what is popular in the class and why.
• Assessment: Check that students can give clear reasons in writing and speaking.
outcomes:

title: Lesson 6 (Part 2): Workbook – School Council Email
concepts:
• Task Analysis: An email answering four points: personality, the best thing about you, what you are good at, why the class should choose you.

pre_learning:

• Assessment: Listen to the quality of the feedback; praise specific, helpful comments.
outcomes:
• Give and receive peer feedback on the emails written for homework.
• Classify sentences as personality, hobbies or likes/dislikes, and use quite/very correctly.

Step 1: Language review 12 min
   - Ex 1: Personality (P), likes/dislikes (LD) or hobby (H)? Answers: 1P, 2LD, 3H, 4LD, 5LD, 6P, 7H.
   - Ex 2: Group adjectives by preposition – at: brilliant, good, terrible; with: bored, fed up; on: keen; in:
interested.
   - Ex 3: quite/very. Answers: 1 quite keen, 2 quite a serious, 3 very confident, 4 very scared, 5 quite interested, 6 very shy.
Step 2: Reading the model 8 min
   - Ex 4: Read the school council advert. What should you write? (an email) How many points? (four).
   - Ex 5: Read Dana’s email and answer the questions (1 yes, 2 yes, 3 yes – serious, friendly, good at …, 4 quite and very).
Step 3: Writing 17 min

concepts:

• Discuss different ways people communicate and explain the meaning of the quote “It’s good to talk”.

STEP 3

title: Lesson 4 (Part 1): Listening – Communicating with animals
concepts:
• Listening Skill: Predicting information – an article before the gap suggests a noun; age/date suggests a number.
• Topic Vocabulary: behaviour, in the wild, body language, nets, sounds, respect, fear, anger.
• Key Message: Communicating with animals relies on respect, not anger or force.
pre_learning:
• Actions: Ask: Which animal would you like to communicate with, and why? Pairs share, then Ex 1: How do people communicate with animals now? (horses understand commands, birds fly away when you shout …).
• Assessment: Check that students can explain ideas with reasons.
outcomes:
• Predict the type of information missing from notes (number, place, thing, feeling).
• Listen to a talk and complete notes with one or two words, avoiding distractors.
• Explain how humans communicate with horses, dolphins and elephants.
• Role-play an interview with an animal, giving opinions and reasons.
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book p. 30 (Ex 1–5, 7); Audio 2.03; Practice Guide p. 81; board
Step 1: Gist listening 6 min

Step 2: Prediction & note completion 18 min
   - Ex 3: Read the study tip; decide what type of word fits each gap: 1 number (age), 2 place, 3 thing, 4 place/thing, 5 thing, 6 feeling/behaviour.
   - Ex 4–5: Listen twice, then compare in pairs. Answers: 1 12, 2 the wild, 3 body language, 4 (the) nets, 5 sounds, 6 respect.

   - Ex 7: Students choose an animal (e.g. a cat or a camel), plan answers about how humans treat it, then role- play an interview in pairs (one is the journalist, one the animal).

closing: Groups discuss which animals have the most “personality” and give one example of how they show feelings (e.g. a cat purrs when relaxed).

title: Lesson 5 (Part 1): Speaking – Describing a photo
concepts:
• Speaking Skill: Fluency ≠ speed; it means speaking with few pauses and little repetition.
• Useful Language: This photo shows … / In the background … / The girl on the left is wearing … / I think they’re … because … / They might be …
pre_learning:
• Actions: Students list people they speak to every day. In pairs, they talk about three of them and what they usually talk about.
• Assessment: Note how long students can talk before stopping.
outcomes:
• Speak fluently for about a minute (few pauses, little repetition) about a person.
• Organise a photo description: who/where → what they are doing → what they look like → what you think.
• Evaluate a weak model answer and suggest improvements.
• Tell a short story about a conversation with a stranger using past tenses.
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book pp. 31, 58 (Ex 1–6); Audio 2.04; Practice Guide p. 85; board
Step 1: Talking at length 8 min
   - Ex 1: Pairs discuss the questions (people in queues, shop assistants, teachers) with a reason and an example.
   - Ex 2: Students choose a topic and speak for one minute; the partner counts pauses. Discuss what fluency means.
Step 2: Organising a description 14 min
   - Ex 3: Make notes on photo A using the questions and the explore language stages (where? what objects? how do they feel? what are they wearing?).

Step 3: Practice task & story 15 min
   - Ex 5: A/B pairs – Student A describes the photo on p. 58, Student B describes photo B on p. 31 for about a minute each.

formative: Peer checklist during Ex 5: the listener ticks each stage used (place, people, actions, appearance, opinion) and gives one suggestion. The teacher gives whole-class feedback on fluency and organisation.
closing: One-minute challenge: a few volunteers describe a photo from the textbook without stopping; the class gives one positive comment each time.
homework: Find a photo of people at home or in a magazine and write 5–6 sentences describing it using: This photo shows … / In the background … / I think they're … because …

title: Lesson 6 (Part 1): Writing – A Story
concepts:
• Strong Adjectives: very funny → hilarious, very bad → disgusting, really big → huge, so sad → miserable, really good → fantastic, very good (food) → delicious.
• Strong Adverbs: absolutely + strong adjective (absolutely fantastic); really/very + normal adjective.
• Story Structure: Beginning (set the scene, past continuous) → middle (events, past simple) → end (result and feelings).
pre_learning:
• Actions: Write happy, embarrassed, exhausted, excited, nervous, scared on the board. In groups, students say what makes them feel each emotion.
• Assessment: Check vocabulary for feelings needed for story writing.
outcomes:
• Identify and correct mistakes in social-media captions.
• Use past simple and past continuous to sequence events in a story.
• Create atmosphere with strong adjectives and adverbs (hilarious, miserable, absolutely, really).
• Plan and write a 100-word story with a clear beginning, middle and end, continuing a given first line.
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book pp. 32–33 (Ex 1–15); Practice Guide p. 75; board
Step 1: Captions & model story 12 min
   - Ex 1–3: Discuss social media posts; correct the preposition errors in the captions (I’m on holiday again / … so easy to make …) and match them to photos.
   - Ex 5: Which tenses tell the main events (past simple) and the background (past continuous)?
   - Ex 6–7: Read the story and choose the correct verbs. Answers: 1 gave, 2 made, 3 were waiting, 4 was feeling/felt, 5 spoke, 6 was presenting, 7 picked up, 8 did, 9 thanked.
Step 2: Strong adjectives 10 min
   - Ex 8: Why miserable and not sad? Find strong adjectives (brilliant, fantastic, miserable) and adverbs (absolutely, really).
   - Ex 9: Replace the words. Answers: 1 hilarious, 2 disgusting, 3 huge, 4 miserable, 5 fantastic, 6 delicious.
   - Ex 10: Pairs tell a short story using strong adjectives.
Step 3: Plan and write 15 min
   - Ex 11: Task analysis – the first line must come first; about 100 words; the reader is your teacher.
   - Ex 12–13: Choose a first line; plan beginning, middle and end; list strong adjectives to use.
   - Ex 14: Start writing in class and finish for homework. Ex 15 (Improve it) will be done next lesson.
formative: Plan check: before writing, students show their plan to a partner, who confirms it has a beginning, middle and end and at least three strong adjectives.
closing: Groups tell their story ideas orally in one minute each and find one thing their stories have in common.
homework: Write a 100-word story continuing the first line from the lesson, with a clear beginning, middle and end, using past simple, past continuous and at least three strong adjectives.

title: Lesson 1 (Part 1): Reading – The future of entertainment
concepts:
• Reading Task: Gapped text – read the sentences before and after each gap; look for pronouns, examples and linking ideas.
• Vocabulary: transform, regularly, preference, version, create, lifelike, consume, challenge, virtual influencer, interactive.
• Critical Thinking: Is AI your friend? – benefits and risks of technology.
pre_learning:
• Actions: Write The future is … . on the board and elicit the missing word (now). Then write Is AI your friend? Pairs list two ways AI helps them and one possible danger. Opener: identify the VR headset in the photo and discuss the questions.
• Assessment: Check students can give balanced opinions (benefits vs dangers).
outcomes:
• Discuss the benefits and dangers of AI and modern technology in daily life.
• Skim an article to identify its topic before doing a detailed task.
• Complete a gapped text by using links between sentences (reference words, ideas before and after the gap).
• Evaluate predictions about the future of entertainment and present a group idea.
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book pp. 37–39 (Opener, Ex 1–8); Practice Guide p. 69; board
Step 1: Pre-reading 8 min
   - This or that: students choose between four leisure activities and justify their choice to a partner.
   - Ex 1–2: Pairs discuss the photo and questions about films, books and screens; predict how entertainment will change.
Step 2: Skim & gapped text 17 min
   - Ex 3: Read the study tip; skim the article – what is it about? (AI in films, virtual characters on social media, making your own films, jobs).
   - Ex 4: Complete the gaps. Answers: 1C, 2H, 3A, 4F, 5D. For each answer, students point to the linking words (e.g. Such characters → virtual influencers).
   - Support for less confident students: tell them sentences B, E and G do not fit.
Step 3: Vocabulary, summary & speaking 12 min
   - Ex 5: Answers: 1 transform, 2 regularly, 3 preference, 4 version, 5 create, 6 lifelike, 7 consume, 8 challenge. Elicit other word forms (transformation, creative …).
   - Ex 6 (Sum up): Explain in your own words three ways AI will change entertainment.
   - Ex 7–8: Pairs evaluate the predictions (… would be good because … / One problem would be …), then groups invent a new form of entertainment and present it.
formative: Justify-the-gap: random students explain the clue that helped them choose each sentence in Ex 4; the class decides if the reasoning is correct.
closing: Pairs choose two topics (a sports star I’d like to meet, a book I like, a type of film I can’t stand …) and speak for 30 seconds each.
homework: Learn the new reading vocabulary (transform, preference, lifelike, interactive …) and write five sentences about the future of entertainment using five of the words.

title: Lesson 2 (Part 1): Grammar – Talking about the future
concepts:
• will: Predictions based on opinion (AI will change films) / immediate decisions (I’ll help you).
• be going to: Intentions (I’m going to start running) / predictions from evidence (Look at the clouds – it’s going to rain).
• Present continuous / simple: Arrangements (I’m meeting my cousin at 5) / timetables (The show starts at 8).
pre_learning:
• Actions: Closed books. In pairs, students talk about their plans for this evening, tomorrow and the weekend. The teacher listens and notes the future forms used.
• Assessment: Diagnostic: which future forms students already use correctly.
outcomes:
• Choose the correct future form: will (opinions, immediate decisions), be going to (intentions, evidence-based predictions), present continuous (arrangements), present simple (timetables).
• Listen to teenagers talking about the future and identify the form and its use.
• Complete an article with appropriate future forms.
• Talk about plans, arrangements and predictions accurately.
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book p. 40 (Ex 1–6); Audio 3.01; Grammar file SB pp. 56–57; board
Step 1: Presenting the forms 12 min
   - Ex 1: Recall the article – what will change? (AI is going to change films …).
   - Ex 2: Match the sentences with the uses. Answers: 1F (present simple – schedule), 2E (present continuous
   - arrangement), 3A (will – opinion), 4D (going to – evidence), 5C (going to – intention), 6B (will – immediate decision).
Step 2: Listening 12 min
   - Ex 3: Play Audio 3.01 – match the questions: A5, B1, C3.
   - Ex 4: Choose the forms, then listen to check. Answers: 1 will watch, 2 will change, 3 I’ll probably, 4 will change, 5 will change, 6 we’re going, 7 will start, 8 am going to visit, 9 I’m meeting, 10 I’m going to iron. Step 3: Article & speaking 13 min
   - Ex 5 (hologram comedian): Answers: 1 starts, 2 will go, 3 are going to enjoy, 4 is going to change, 5 will see, 6 will always be.
   - Ex 6: Pairs talk about the four prompts (a chore, an appointment, a plan, a prediction about yourself) using the correct forms and asking follow-up questions.
formative: Function cards: the teacher reads situations (You’ve already bought the ticket. / You suddenly decide to help.). Students show the correct form on paper (PC / will / going to / PS). Discuss any split answers.

concepts:

• Phrasal Verbs: switch on/off, turn up/down, plug in, set up (separable); go off, come on (inseparable).

pre_learning:
• Actions: Teams have two minutes to list technology found in the home. The team with the longest correct list reads it aloud; the class checks.
• Assessment: Check existing vocabulary and spelling.
outcomes:
• Name and correctly stress words for household appliances.
• Understand and use phrasal verbs for technology (switch on/off, turn up/down, plug in, set up, go off, come on).

activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book p. 41 (Ex 1–7); Practice Guide p. 71; board
Step 1: Appliances 8 min
   - Ex 1: Label the photos: A kettle, B microwave, C TV, D fridge-freezer, E washing machine, F dishwasher, G coffee maker, H speaker, I air conditioning. Mark the stress.
   - Ex 2: Pairs agree on the three most useful appliances and justify.
Step 2: Phrasal verbs 14 min
   - Ex 3: Match the phrasal verbs with the meanings. Answers: 1D, 2H, 3B, 4A, 5F, 6E, 7C, 8G.
   - Ex 4: Read explore language – all are separable except go off and come on.
   - Board check: Don’t forget your shoes – take off them ✗ → take them off ✓.
   - Ex 5: Pairs say which sentences are true for them (e.g. I always switch off the lights – it saves electricity).
Step 3: Cloze & speaking 15 min
   - Ex 6: Answers: 1B, 2B, 3C, 4A (connect to), 5D, 6C (reminds). Students explain why the other options are wrong.
   - Ex 7: Pairs think of a problem at home and invent a smart device to solve it; present it to the class.
formative: Drawing game: a student draws a clue on the board (e.g. plug and socket); the class guesses the phrasal verb and uses it in a sentence with a pronoun in the correct position.
closing: Discuss: How smart is your home? What will homes be like in thirty years? Each student makes one prediction using will.

title: Lesson 5 (Part 1): Speaking – Collaborative task & discussion
concepts:
• Giving Opinions: In my opinion, In my view, For me, I think / don’t think, I’d say …
• Asking: What’s your view on …? What do you think?
• Agreeing / Disagreeing: That’s a good point. / You’re right. / I disagree. / That’s true, but … / I’m not sure.
pre_learning:
• Actions: Students close their eyes and imagine a robot: What does it look like? What does it do? Pairs describe their robots and compare. Ex 1: discuss what a robot could do for you.
• Assessment: Check descriptive language and opinions.
outcomes:
• Give and ask for opinions, and agree or disagree politely.
• Listen to two candidates and identify which AI assistant they choose and why.
• Discuss options with a partner and try to reach a decision (B1 Preliminary Speaking Part 3 style).
• Answer follow-up discussion questions about technology with reasons.
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book pp. 43, 59, 61 (Ex 1–8); Audio 3.03; Practice Guide pp. 87, 89; board
Step 1: Listening to a model 10 min
   - Ex 2: Play Audio 3.03 – which AI assistants do they discuss? (household, doctor, clothes) Which do they choose? (clothes assistant – it helps you feel confident).
   - Ex 3: Complete the extracts. Answers: 1 opinion, true; 2 view, disagree; 3 on, sure; 4 say, good; 5 For, right.

title: Lesson 6 (Part 1): Writing – An Email giving advice
concepts:
• Writing Skill: Giving advice and suggestions: I think you ought to … / You should … / Why don’t you …? / You could … / How about …?
• Organisation: Paragraph 1 – respond to the news; Paragraph 2 – advice; Paragraph 3 – your own plan; friendly ending.
• Style: Informal: Hi …, contractions, friendly phrases.
pre_learning:
• Actions: Pairs discuss: Who do you go to when you need help with technology? Do you ever help others? Who?
• Assessment: Check students can talk about helping others with reasons.
outcomes:
• Read a notice and an email and identify all the points the reply must include.
• Analyse a model email for paragraphing and informal style.
• Use a range of phrases to give advice and make suggestions.
• Plan and write an informal email of about 100 words answering four prompts.
activities_teach:
Materials: Student’s Book pp. 44–45 (Ex 1–12); Practice Guide p. 73; board
Step 1: Reading the task & model 12 min
   - Ex 1: Predict what Teen Tech Help Month is; read the notice and discuss the questions.
   - Ex 2–3: Why is Arwa writing? What four things must Jood include? Does she include them all? (yes).
   - Ex 4: Analyse Jood’s email – three paragraphs; informal style (Hi, contractions).
Step 2: Advice language 10 min
   - Ex 5: Identify the function of the highlighted phrases: expressing concern, giving advice, making suggestions, giving a reason.
   - Ex 6: Complete the prompts with suggestions for Jood (You should help older people use their phones. / How about helping people set up websites?).
Step 3: Plan and write 15 min
   - Ex 7–8: Read Khalid’s email, answer the questions and plan the reply in paragraphs.
   - Ex 9: Write the email (about 100 words) – start in class, finish for homework.
   - Ex 10–12 (Improve it): self-check questions, rewrite weak parts, read twice (meaning, then accuracy).
formative: Plan swap: partners check that the plan covers all four prompts and includes at least two different advice phrases before writing begins.
closing: Groups predict how technology will change transport, healthcare, education and communication, and choose one prediction they are sure will come true.
homework: Write an informal email of about 100 words answering the four prompts from the lesson, using at least three advice phrases (You should …, Why don't you …?, How about …?).
